implementation-timeline.label: Implementation Timeline
implementation-timeline.title: Live in 90 Days, ROI in 120
heading: Discovery & Data Audit
Platform Rollout & Automation
Cutover & First ROI Benchmark
body:
We map your existing HR and IT stack end-to-end — every payroll provider, benefits broker, identity tool, and device manager.

Your employee census is imported, and we configure SSO and directory sync so Rippling becomes the single source of truth from day one.

Payroll, benefits, and device management go live on the unified platform. App provisioning rules are configured by role so the right tools reach the right people automatically.

Managers and admins complete training to self-serve on workflows they previously filed tickets for.

Legacy systems are decommissioned after a parallel payroll run confirms accuracy. The employee self-service portal launches company-wide, eliminating routine HR requests.

By week 12, we benchmark your first ROI — customers at 1,000 employees typically see $340K/yr in savings.

heading: Every satisfying AI demo today runs on someone else's infrastructure...
...so the next wave of durable companies will be built on proprietary data, not better prompts.
body:
The AI market is repeating a pattern we've seen three times before. In cloud, mobile, and SaaS, early winners built point solutions on shared infrastructure — then got commoditized when the platform layer consolidated.

Right now, 80% of AI startups rely on the same three foundation model providers, gross margins average 50–60% (vs. 70–80% for mature SaaS), and the majority of venture funding is flowing to the model layer, not the application layer.

The window for differentiation is narrowing fast.

We're transitioning from Phase 1 (point solutions) to Phase 2 (platforms) of AI market evolution. The companies that survive consolidation will be the ones acquiring proprietary data loops now — before the infrastructure layer locks in.

1. Embed into workflows where you capture unique data with every interaction.

2. Build compounding moats that model providers can't replicate.

3. Target verticals where domain-specific data is scarce and defensible.

fullbleed-image-left-title-paragraph-rig.subtitle: Creating with intention means being thoughtful about every interaction, every visual, and every feature. Great ideas deserve tools that stay out of the way and help you think better, not louder. That's why the product is designed to support flow, reduce friction, and bring clarity to the creative process — so you can move from messy thinking to sharp output without losing momentum or purpose.
text: Intentional design isn't just about how things look. It's about how they work, how they feel, and how they respect your time and attention. It's a quiet discipline that values clarity over flash and function over filler. It means stripping away what's unnecessary to make room for what truly matters. It's in the pacing of an interface, the rhythm of a layout, the way an idea flows from start to finish without friction. When design is purposeful, it doesn't demand your focus. It supports it. It helps you move more naturally, think more clearly, and feel more in control. Because when the tools you use are considered and calm, your work has the space to become sharper, deeper, and more meaningful.

body: Blasting “Hey, upvote us!” in a Slack community you joined yesterday smells spammy and converts <1%. Show up where you already have social credit.
Flash floods from brand-new accounts triggered grey-vote purges for some; we steered clear. Quality > quantity every single time.
Engagement dilutes fast; two cinematic, BTS-packed threads out-perform a dozen low-effort tweets that push followers to mute.
A launch thread is a live stage: unanswered questions = walk-outs. We replied through the day.
Ads. Veterans warned us that paid traffic on launch day rarely converts; we skipped ads and don’t regret it.

statement-a16z-two-title-paragraph-with-.title: Every shift follows a pattern
statement-a16z-two-title-paragraph-with-.subtitle: Developer conference talk
text:
Every major platform shift from cloud computing to mobile to SaaS has followed the same predictable four-phase arc: fragmented point solutions emerge first, then platforms consolidate, data moats form, and finally infrastructure hardens. 
AI is now transitioning from phase one to phase two, the critical inflection where winners and losers are decided. The data is clear — 72% of AI startups depend on the same three model providers, margins average 50–60% versus the 70–80% SaaS benchmark, and $42B in funding remains concentrated at the infrastructure layer. The window to build proprietary data loops is closing fast.

title-global-electricity-mix-2025.title: What powered the world's electricity in 2025
title-global-electricity-mix-2025.subtitle: For the first time in over a century, renewables overtook coal — and solar alone delivered more new generation than every other source combined.

chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: Ember Global Electricity Review 2026, IEA 2025

heading: Coal lost its century-long crown
Solar delivered the surge
Nuclear started its comeback
Gas grew where renewables stalled
Low-carbon sources crossed 42%
body: Coal's share fell below 33% for the first time in 100 years, as renewables overtook it in the first half of 2025 — the structural shift the energy transition has been waiting for.
Solar generation grew by 636 TWh in 2025, the single largest annual increase from any electricity source in history. Solar alone covered 83% of the rise in global demand.
Over 12 GW of new nuclear reactor construction began in 2025, the strongest year for new builds in decades — nuclear's share reached 8.9% with major projects in China, India, and Europe.
Natural gas generation grew most where renewables couldn't keep pace, including Taiwan (where the last reactor shut down) and Türkiye (where the worst drought in 61 years cut hydropower).
Renewables plus nuclear reached 42.6% of global electricity in 2025 — up from 33.5% in 2015. Fossil generation dropped to 57.4%, the lowest share on record.

chart-nvda-title-kagi-chart.title: NVDA — buyers defend every higher low
chart-nvda-title-kagi-chart.subtitle: Over 30 half-hour reversals, up-legs gain $7–8, pullbacks lose $5–6.5. Violent whipsaws but every dip bought higher than the last. Net $132→$155 (+$23, +17.4%) across 29 confirmed reversals. Higher highs and higher lows intact.

chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: illustrative NVDA 30-minute intraday data for template demo.

box-plot-chart-title-intc-monthly-ohlc-s.title: Intel's choppy year, month by month
box-plot-chart-title-intc-monthly-ohlc-s.subtitle: Each box spans the month's open and close, with whiskers marking the full high–low range. Red months closed below where they opened — the run of red through the middle of the year captures Intel's pressured stretch, while the wide whiskers show how volatile individual months were.

candlestick-chart-title-nvda-daily-ohlc.subtitle: Each candle is one trading day — the body spans open to close, the wicks the day's high and low. A red stretch mid-period gives way to a strong green run as the stock rallies back above where it started.

bubble-chart-title-country-development-s.label: Strategic Positioning
bubble-chart-title-country-development-s.title: The AI platform landscape, mapped
bubble-chart-title-country-development-s.subtitle:
Each bubble is a platform plotted by completeness of vision (X) against ability to execute (Y); bubble size is market presence.

The top-right is crowded — execution and vision now travel together. The lonely bottom corners are the real signal: strong vision with weak delivery, or the reverse, rarely survives a full cycle.

chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: illustrative positioning for template demo

scatter-chart-title-rnd-vs-capability.label: Correlation
scatter-chart-title-rnd-vs-capability.title: More R&D buys capability — but not cleanly
scatter-chart-title-rnd-vs-capability.subtitle:
Each point is an AI lab: annual R&D spend (X) against its capability score (Y).

The trend slopes up — bigger budgets do buy stronger models. But the line isn't straight: point 3 spends more than point 2 and scores lower, and point 5 outspends point 4 yet trails it. Money sets the ceiling, not the result.

chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: illustrative positioning for template demo

bump-chart-title-platform-capability-rac.label: Priority Shift
bump-chart-title-platform-capability-rac.title: How enterprise AI priorities reshuffled, 2019–2025
bump-chart-title-platform-capability-rac.subtitle: Data security never loses the top spot. The real movement is underneath: model accuracy and compliance climb into the top three, while the talent gap collapses from #3 to dead last as tooling matures.

chart-text-content.graphictitle: Top enterprise AI concerns, ranked by survey share
chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: illustrative survey data for template demo

column-comparison-chart-title-ai-adoptio.label: Adoption Gap
column-comparison-chart-title-ai-adoptio.title: Who's actually shipping AI to production
column-comparison-chart-title-ai-adoptio.subtitle:
Each bar is the share of firms in that industry running AI in production, not just piloting it.

Technology leads at 52% — more than triple the public sector. The pattern isn't about ambition, it's about friction: the most regulated and legacy-heavy industries sit at the bottom, and that's where the next wave of adoption has to come from.

chart-text-content.sourcetext: Source: illustrative adoption data for template demo
